title: Consumer Financial Protection Circular 2022-03: Adverse action notification requirements in connection with credit decisions based on complex algorithms

covered_actors: Creditors making credit decisions using complex algorithms, artificial intelligence, or machine learning

Federal and state authorities enforcing federal consumer financial law (CFPB, state attorneys general, state regulators, FDIC, OCC, Federal Reserve, NCUA, DOJ, FTC, Farm Credit Administration, DOT, USDA)
prohibited_practices: Using complex, uninterpretable, or 'black-box' algorithms in credit decisions when doing so prevents the creditor from providing specific and accurate principal reasons for adverse actions under ECOA and Regulation B

Discriminating against any credit applicant on prohibited bases under ECOA (15 U.S.C. 1691(a)) including race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age, public assistance income, or good-faith exercise of Consumer Credit Protection Act rights

Issuing generic adverse action notices citing internal policies or failure to achieve a qualifying credit score, or selecting Regulation B Appendix C sample reasons that were not the factors actually considered or scored

evidence.quote: Creditors who use complex algorithms, including artificial intelligence or machine learning, in any aspect of their credit decisions must still provide a notice that discloses the specific principal reasons for taking an adverse action.
Thus, ECOA and Regulation B do not permit creditors to use complex algorithms when doing so means they cannot provide the specific and accurate reasons for adverse actions.

While some creditors may rely upon various post-hoc explanation methods, such explanations approximate models and creditors must still be able to validate the accuracy of those approximations, which may not be possible with less interpretable models.
A creditor’s lack of understanding of its own methods is therefore not a cognizable defense against liability for violating ECOA and Regulation B’s requirements.

Consumer Financial Protection Circulars are issued to all parties with authority to enforce federal consumer financial law. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau
(CFPB) is the principal federal regulator responsible for administering federal consumer financial law, see 12 U.S.C. 5511

Consumer Financial Protection Circulars are general statements of policy under the Administrative Procedure Act. 5 U.S.C. 553(b). They provide background information about applicable law, articulate considerations relevant to the Bureau's exercise of its authorities, and, in the interest of maintaining consistency, advise other parties with authority to enforce federal consumer financial law.

enforcement_authorities: State attorneys general and state regulators
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
policy_extraction.penalties_summary: Clarifies that a creditor's inability to explain its own complex or 'black-box' algorithm is not a cognizable defense against liability for violating ECOA (15 U.S.C. 1691) and Regulation B (12 CFR 1002.9), enforceable by the CFPB, state attorneys general, prudential regulators, DOJ, FTC, other federal agencies, and private plaintiffs. As an APA general statement of policy, the Circular itself imposes no new standalone legal requirements or penalties.
policy_extraction.implementation_notes: Issued May 26, 2022 as an APA general statement of policy (5 U.S.C. 553(b)) promoting enforcement consistency across federal and state consumer financial enforcers. Confirms that ECOA and Regulation B written adverse action notice duties apply equally regardless of model complexity, that disclosing FCRA credit-score factors or generic sample checklist reasons does not satisfy ECOA unless they reflect the actual principal factors scored, and that creditors using post-hoc explanation methods must validate the accuracy of those approximations.

risk_framing.rationale_summary: CFPB Circular 2022-03 is dominantly framed around fundamental_rights, grounding adverse action explainability mandates in the Equal Credit Opportunity Act's anti-discrimination protections across protected classes and procedural fairness enabling applicants to detect and challenge credit errors. Fundamental_rights narrowly edges out consumer_public_safety because preventing discrimination ex ante is highlighted as the core statutory purpose of ECOA's notice rule. Consumer_public_safety is a very strong runner-up, explicitly invoking ECOA's 'twin goals of consumer protection and education' and the CFPB's mandate against unfair, deceptive, and abusive practices, while economic_competitiveness plays a minor supporting role via Congress's view that notice rules have a beneficial competitive effect on the credit marketplace.

evidence_spans.quote: ECOA makes it unlawful for any creditor to discriminate against any applicant, with respect to any aspect of a credit transaction, on the basis of race, color, religion, national origin, sex or

In terms of consumer protection, “the notice requirement is intended to prevent discrimination ex ante because ‘if creditors know they must explain their decisions . . . they [will] effectively be discouraged’ from discriminatory practices.”
ECOA’s notice requirements “were designed to fulfill the twin goals of consumer protection and education.”

As a result of being informed of the specific reasons for the adverse action, consumers can take steps to try to improve their credit status or, in cases “where the creditor may have acted on misinformation or inadequate information[,] . . . to rectify the mistake.”
In addition, Congress also believed ECOA’s notice requirement would have “a beneficial competitive effect on the credit marketplace.”
